response:
[1] Aching and swelling two to three months after knee replacement: Two to three months after a knee replacement, the knee usually feels much better than it did in the first weeks, but it is still healing. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that mild to moderate swelling can last for about three to six months after surgery, so it is common for the knee to look a little puffy after a busy day or a long walk. Some aching with activity is normal at this stage, and the knee can still feel stiff when you bend it a long way. Kneeling may be uncomfortable; it is not harmful to the new joint, but NHS guidance is to wait for your doctor's go-ahead before kneeling on the new knee. Continuing your exercises matters.
[2] Two to three months after knee replacement: work and fuller activity: A useful sign of progress is being able to manage everyday lower-body tasks such as putting on socks and tying shoelaces, and climbing stairs step over step with little pain. Mild to moderate swelling may still come and go, and it can last for about three to six months. NHS guidance is still to avoid heavy lifting at home, such as vacuuming or carrying shopping, until about three months. Recovery continues well beyond this point; full recovery from a knee replacement can take several months or longer, and the pace varies with age and general health, so do not be discouraged if the knee is not yet as strong or flexible as you hoped. Keep attending your follow-up appointments and raise any concerns about your progress with your team.
[3] Is my knee recovery on track? What steady progress looks like: Useful markers from the HSS guideline are about 80 degrees of bending by the end of the first week, more than 110 degrees with a fully straight knee by around six weeks, and more than 120 degrees for people aiming to return to demanding activities, but your own team's targets take priority. A knee that is still swollen and stiff at four to six weeks is common and does not by itself mean recovery is slow, because mild to moderate swelling can last three to six months. Talk to your physiotherapist or surgeon if your range of motion stops improving or the end of the bend feels hard and painful, if you cannot straighten the knee fully, if pain is increasing rather than decreasing, or if you cannot progress your walking.
[4] The months ahead after knee replacement: Recovery from a knee replacement continues for months after the early rehabilitation period, and NHS guidance says it can take several months or longer to recover fully. Mild to moderate swelling may persist for about three to six months, especially after activity. It is common to have a patch of numb skin near the scar and some stiffness, particularly when bending the knee a long way. Kneeling can feel uncomfortable, although it does not damage the implant; check with your doctor before you start kneeling on the new knee. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons advises continuing your prescribed exercises for at least two months after surgery and building activity up gradually rather than doing too much, too soon.
